# Here begins the Book of Archelaus <gloss>119</gloss> <gloss>Here begins the book of Archelaus’s alchemy</gloss> on alchemy
<gloss>In the name of the blessed Lord, I, Archelaus, explain</gloss>

<margin>+</margin>This book definitively treats the mineral work and the greater work <note>original: "min'alis opis & maioris"; the "lesser work" or mineral work typically refers to the creation of silver, while the "greater work" refers to the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone and gold.</note>. And in this thing, the secrets of all the philosophers are revealed in great detail <note>original: "r'ngi ī m' & ō theniū"; likely *regni in multis et omnium*</note>. This is the complete summary of this treatise, which has exhausted all other books of teaching; in it are those things which he wished to include in his previous books. Those who wish to perform such works—unless they are the "children of knowledge" <note>original: "filij agniē" (filii agnitionis); a common alchemical term for initiated students or "sons of the art."</note>—will not have these things appear to them.

Here are the signs of transmutation and the hours, days, and methods:
The book of decoction <term>decoction|The process of "cooking" or heating a substance in a fluid to extract its essence or mature it.</term>, its time and method. 
The book of weights and how to weigh.
The book of fire and the book of vessels.
The book of furnaces and the method of the book of calcination <term>calcination|The process of heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures to reduce it to a brittle powder or ash.</term>.
The true method of the book of the preparation of metals.
The method of the book of sulfur <note>original: "sulph'is"; sulfur was considered the "father" of metals in alchemical theory.</note>, both common and red.
The method of the book of alums, of ammonia, and of tartar <note>original: "tartar'im"; cream of tartar or potassium bitartrate, often used as a flux.</note>.
The method of the book of atrament <note>original: "at'm'tis"; vitriol or black metallic inks.</note> and the method of the book of common salt.
The method of the book of saltpeter <note>original: "sal' nit'"; potassium nitrate.</note> and the method of the book of Indian salt.
The method of the book of salt of vitriol: violet, acetic <note>original: "accē" (acetum); vinegar-like or acid.</note>, red, and white.
The method of the book of the preparation of chicken eggs for few colors, and of pheasant eggs for many colors. 
Concerning the aforementioned colors: <insert>After this, mention will be made of</insert> the preparation of the finest papers <note>original: "cartū' s'mū'"; possibly referring to the preparation of "cards" or "papers" used to test chemical reactions or colors.</note> proceeding toward the other mentioned things. To reach the highest secrets, namely those concerning the twelve minerals that melt between other minerals <unclear>f'uati</unclear> and the acrid spirits.

<insert>Then the book of the 12 waters <note>original: "12 az'"; refers to the *Twelve Waters*, a famous medieval alchemical text describing various corrosive or transformative liquids.</note>, than which no better is found in this world.</insert>
<insert>After this, it will speak of the whitening of eggs,</insert> the resolution <note>original: "resolōe"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note> of the highest teachings: how wine may be frozen <note>original: "g'elē vinu'"; likely referring to the concentration of alcohol or the crystallization of tartar.</note> without long grinding, and the manner in which it is coagulated with distillation, and the manner of purification in horse dung <term>horse dung|A standard alchemical heat source; the natural fermentation of the dung provided a gentle, steady warmth for "digesting" substances over many days.</term>. These lead from the actions to the true things and the moisture of tin, and the exposure to the Sun and to the Moon <note>original: "ad solē & ad lunā"; referring to the gold and silver stages of the work.</note>. This work is called the Divine Science <note>original: "d'i' cacīa"; possibly a corruption of *divina kemia* or *divina acacia*.</note>. After this, many experiments of the first men are presented for the perfecting of the work of alchemy, which are easily collected in their regions.

Having completed these various preparations regarding the minerals, it is then translated to the divine crystals and others explained in the series of the work. But in turn, because these things were understood by the son <unclear>uce'</unclear> far from all greed, this book is completed in the common book of minerals.

He spoke and said <note>original: "passa & dixit"; likely referring to a vision or a guiding figure</note>, and he set my path toward a certain city, saying: "Enter the returning city <note>original: "ciuitatē reūtē"; this may refer to a city being restored or a spiritual 'return' to knowledge.</note> and set your face toward its purity." Let it be called upon, for it helped because of the day of the people's eyes <note>meaning: for the sake of public enlightenment</note>. Through these things, the secrets of the world were opened by God to a pure person—all the communicable and transferable secrets of the world, by the gift of the Most High: **Necromancy**, **Geometry**, **Arithmetic**, **Geomancy**, **Astronomy**, **Physiognomy**, and the **Mathematical art**, stating which are good and which are evil. These are also found among other Arabs, which certainly are seen in their own books regarding God.

**O**, if only those things which were then foretold to me [had been brought] to the Emperor of Constantinople, who is called **Emanuel** <note>Emperor Manuel I Komnenos, who ruled 1143–1180 and was a famous patron of the occult and alchemical sciences.</note>. He, in a most Christian manner, sought how much you might be able to stay with him, for he likewise will freely fulfill all your good instructions. And he said: "Go, go with God’s blessing." And wonderment came upon me. I swear by my soul, as I intend to render the truth to God, that from the heights, that pilgrim <note>original: "peḡrnus"; Archelaus often refers to himself or his guide as a pilgrim.</note> finished [speaking] in a clear voice; through the good God, he then narrated and gave counsel for the sake of good. 

And I set out toward my home. Before I, a pilgrim man, arrived in Constantinople, the way was falling away from me <note>likely meaning he felt lost or the path was difficult</note>, but I was at the beginning and in peace... through the hands of my whole family, through my king, [I was] offered [the way] in which all the instructions of the pilgrim were contained. And I came to the city of Constantinople, to the Emperor, and I showed him my hands and feet <note>likely a metaphor for showing the results of his labor or his physical presence as a servant</note>. He received me, and the barons or nobles provided for me with a gift. 

Through this, I then began to say that [strength is] not in [men], but in God alone. In the highest God, I arranged for salvation by the power and help of our Lord Jesus Christ. **And** furthermore, I have deleted the names of all the compositions of the **Greater and Lesser Elixir** <term>Elixir|original: "elinū" (elixir); in alchemy, the Greater Elixir (Philosopher's Stone) was for transmuting metals, while the Lesser was for silver.</term>, and I have done well, because they were hidden by a few [scholars] with bonds. They hid them because they seemed trivial, and were held by very few. But I have revealed everything out of love for the Divine Emperor **Emanuel**, who petitioned me, and out of love for the poor, so that this summary might be completed prosperously.

# Amalgamation of the Laconic [Metal].

### The Calcining of Tin
<margin>Scoria <note>original: "Schturia" — dross or slag</note>. Take... before you, it was made to turn elsewhere, all the lumps made in the same way for the calcining of lead... as much as the Laconic amalgam then leaves... <note>The marginal note is heavily abbreviated and concerns the recycling of metallic dross.</note></margin>
**T**ake of tin <term>stagnū<span>A common alchemical term for tin, often associated with the planet Jupiter.</span></term> as much as you wish, melt it and let it cool. [Take] ten measures of lime water and [some] water dissolved in sharp vinegar; let it sit. [Take] two parts of honey and grind it there; when it is well ground, [add] alkali salt <term>sal xacen<span>Likely "sal alkali" or "sal saracenicum," a caustic salt used as a flux.</span></term> and... and if it floats, [add] the aforementioned honey. It should be stained until it is dark; then put it in a pot in a bread oven <note>original: "furno panis" — used for steady, moderate heat</note> or among the coals for a natural day. Extract the lime of the moon <term>calce lune<span>A term for silver or a purified white metallic powder.</span></term> when it is not yet ready. <gloss>calcining of tin</gloss>

### Concerning Iron
**T**his is concerning iron, which... and when it breaks... and [is] dissolved in water of sal ammoniac <term>sal armōniac<span>Ammonium chloride, used to clean metal surfaces or as a volatile agent in reactions.</span></term>... for ten times... salt... afterward it is born outside from the water... put it [in the heat] ten times. <gloss>which dissolves all things in the water...</gloss> Let the water freeze for a natural day by the benefit [of the heat] and the sharp winds. Add salt... Then take iron filings and grind them well; put them in the oven for a day and a night, until you find a red lime <note>original: "calce rubā" — likely iron oxide or "crocus martis"</note> that has its use. Farewell.

### Concerning the Lime of Silver
<margin>Concerning the calcining of silver...</margin>
**T**ake silver and make it into thin sheets; [use] triple-strength iron tongs, placing them on a tablet of salt... until it is fully covered... grind it well and put it in a bread oven for a natural day. Extract the lime of the moon <note>original: "calce lune"</note> when it is not ready.

### Concerning the Lime of Gold
**T**ake gold or make thin sheets... cover it on an iron plate and let it melt with salt and a little sal ammoniac in sharp vinegar... or use alkali salt. Grind it... then put it in a bread oven for a natural day. Extract the red lime <note>original: "calce rubrā" — gold powder was often called red lime or "calx solis"</note>.
<margin>Note that... the authors of this art... <note>This marginal note appears to be a scholarly citation or a warning about the process.</note></margin>
...it is not ready; [it is] a soluble lime. <gloss>Thus it says that it must be washed</gloss> of the flavors and the whiteness of the alkali salt... and it should be dissolved and congealed... in the lime.

### Concerning the Lime of Copper
<margin>Concerning the lime of copper...</margin>
**T**ake sheets of copper and put them in vinegar or the dregs of wine; having placed them in a pot, put them in the highest heat for ten days. Extract that which you find... until the sheets are finished. Then wash them in vinegar and dry them carefully. When you see the vinegar-water, it will look very green; strain it... then let it reside and strain it again. [By bathing it] you will see... then the green color is greatly increased; put it in the sun and bathe it more, and purify it as if it were floating...

**T**hese [preparations] of tin, which you wish to be made... and the lime of gold... in the sun during the Dog Days <note>original: "dieb' canicularib'" — the hottest days of summer, associated with the star Sirius</note>... with salt water, vinegar, and alum water. However, if it is for the Moon [Silver], and if it is for the Sun [Gold], then [use] water of sal ammoniac... then you will have it.

# Sublimation of mercury for the Whiteness <note>original: "ad albedo"</note>
Take one part of <unclear>clear</unclear> <unclear>crystals</unclear> which are white... with three parts of alum, and with the same amount of salt with <unclear>vinegar</unclear>... so that it is all made into a paste, and let it remain in a mortar until it is seen to be [well-mixed]. **S**ublime the <term>sulfur</term><note>Sulfur was viewed by alchemists as the "soul" or active combustible principle of metals.</note> and the gold. The earth is brought to the state of glass <note>original: "yez," likely referring to vitrification or a vitriolic salt</note> from the sulfur.

I have described these corrections of various sulfates at length in the book which is called "The Veins of Digestion" <note>original: "vēis ī ī digeſtūis," possibly referring to a specific alchemical treatise on the "maturation" of metals</note>, where one can see many waters that can be purified. **T**he <term>ablution</term><note>A technical term for the ceremonial or chemical "washing" of a substance to remove impurities.</note> of Lead <note>original: "plub̃i," referring to the metal associated with Saturn</note> is done through expression and a little washing, extracting the white essence from the salt.

**M**elt the <term>Dragon's Blood</term><note>original: "s̃agũũ," likely *sanguis draconis*, a bright red resin used as a pigment and in alchemical tinctures.</note> and do not let it touch the salt water. **T**he washing of Iron <note>original: "mart̃is," the metal of Mars</note> should be done with a portion of its own gold.

# The Procedure for Calcined Materials

The process for **calcined materials** <term>calcined materials: substances reduced to powder by heat, usually metallic oxides</term> proceeds in this way: Let us take a sufficient amount of the material, specifically the red <note>original: "roseis primis," possibly referring to red lead or another "first" red stage in the work</note> before it is calcined. Then take vinegar and let it be purified. Afterward, take the dried material—though still slightly moist—and pour the **calcinated water** over it in a vessel, so that it might dissolve from the calx. 

Then, strain it through a filter <note>original: "per annum miera," likely a corruption of "per amnum/pannum," through a cloth or filter</note> in the sun. Or, boil it first with water until the water is reduced by boiling. When it is combined, take **salt** and work it into both until the saltiness hardens. Agitate it with water while it dissolves.

Take the **Eagle** <term>Eagle: "aquila," the alchemical code for Sal Ammoniac (ammonium chloride)</term> with vinegar, and take all the spirit that is held in the vinegar. While it boils, dry the earth until it is no longer lead-colored <note>original: "non blum," likely meaning "non plumbeum," not leaden</note> but becomes white. Afterward, distill this white material. Take the water and let it stand for several days. Finally, strain and distill it; take as much as you wish of that which distills, as the **philosophers** <note>referring to the "Adepts" or ancient alchemical authorities</note> say.

## Of the Second Water and Aqua Fortis

Likewise, for the **second water**, take vinegar and distill it. <margin>1.5 lbs of vitriol</margin> Take half of the distilled vinegar and add it to the second water. Then take the **Gold** <term>Gold: "aurum" or "sol," the Sun</term> and pour the said water over it. Distill it, and in that same hour, the second water will transform the calx.

If the water is what is called **"Water of Calagnum"** <note>likely a specific local or proprietary name for a corrosive solution</note>, take it and distill it. Straining it produces the **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," or nitric acid</term>. With this, you may do what you wish. 

There is also the "Water of the Earth," which is a water made through itself. Take the white material, distill it without salt until it boils, and mix it with the distillate. Cook it with moisture. Distill it until the water sustains what is called **Claret** <note>meaning a clear, clarified liquid, though often used for spiced wine, here it refers to alchemical clarity</note>. 

### Of Corrosive Waters

Likewise, **Hippocrates** <note>the text attributes this to the ancient Greek physician, a common practice to lend authority to recipes</note> says of this: over any wine, it will distill with the water of calagnum. Take this water and it will dissolve the **Sun and Moon** <term>Sun and Moon: Gold and Silver</term> in that very hour. 

These are the **burning waters** <term>burning waters: "aquas adurentes," highly corrosive mineral acids</term>. Take vinegar and the scent of lead-earth with salt and the **Gold of the Dead** <note>original: "aurum de mortuorum," likely referring to gold recovered from an alloy or a specific calx of gold</note>. Distill it in such a vessel. Take all the filings and dissolve them with a light fire. When it boils in the light, it becomes white and snowy. This water dissolves the calx in that very hour.

## **R**efined azure or lead red <term>minium|red lead, an orange-red pigment frequently used to fraudulently bulk out expensive blue pigments</term> reduced to a powder, which removes any [impurities]. Item: there is a fire that has not changed its color... toward blackness... toward whiteness in the final artifice.

## **S**i you wish [to test it], put it in your hand... with clear water; likewise, if it is well poured out with the fingers, if it goes through the clouds <note>original: "nuvulas"; likely referring to the way the pigment disperses or "clouds" in water</note> of the hand... New Avignon <note>original: "Auic savelle nove"</note> which is a very beautiful and good azure.

## **S**windlers and deceivers are accustomed to placing red lead in the bottom of the bag... in a good way to expose it to loss... in sharp vinegar... and likewise that which is at the bottom... by nodding thus it is given to you. <note>The text describes a common fraud where expensive blue pigment was layered over cheap red lead to trick the buyer.</note>

## **E**t if the deceivers are particularly clever, they mix red lead and azure with barley or oats to increase the weight... for the purpose of extending the azure... then they have it in a seal or a linen cloth to protect it...

## **A**rtificial azure... take tanner's earth <term>terra pellicaria|a fine clay or earth used in tanning and as a substrate for lake pigments</term> reduced to a powder. Or by way of lime. Or lime made of eggshells. Or lime made of white marble, which is on a porphyry stone... with the flower... the color is added... Likewise, silver plates <note>original: "lamias argenti"</note> made very thin, which you may roll up... suspended over the sharpest vinegar in a pot or another vessel, well-covered, and placed under warm horse dung <note>original: "fimo equo calio"; horse dung was used in alchemy and pigment making as a source of steady, gentle heat</note> for six days... then filter it, and from there comes a very beautiful flower of azure.

## **M**ethod for seeing how a "rose" is made, that is, a very beautiful rose color. Take tanner's earth... make a wide hole in some [vessel]... in the dust of the tanner's earth... and throughout the day move it... white of eggs <note>original: "albu d' pulia"</note>... or by filtering...

## **D**ecoction... a good [mixture]... not oil in a vessel, let it boil... in pure earth... or well-filtered through a linen cloth... from which this work is made; likewise there is a powder of a colored rose color.

## **W**hen
you wish to have a very beautiful rose, scrape it well... likewise... in your horn <note>original: "cornu tuo"; animal horns were commonly used as small containers for prepared pigments</note> and [mix] with egg whites... stirring it with a stick. And by adding some of the best grain lake <term>grana lac|a red dye derived from the lac insect</term>... move it well... the color in the hand... a very beautiful rose.

# Ozar Water

**Take** of the prepared *ozar* <term>ozari|likely a mineral compound, possibly a form of arsenic or mercury such as cinnabar, used as a base for chemical transformation</term> which was spoken of before. Put it into a vial <note>original: "fildo," likely a variant of "fiala"</note> which you can stop up <note>seal</note> well. Put it in a place where it can be well-turned and distill it. Through a moist heat <note>original: "v̄ōm hūīdū"; a vapor bath or gentle heat</note> it will soften <note>original: "dulcet"; literally 'sweeten,' but in alchemy referring to removing corrosiveness or softening a substance</note>. Do not worry about this [the softening], because it is said by certain arts that it is not a true water of *ozar* unless it is refined many times. It is prepared so that the *ozar* dries out, which is done in the furnace for a long time.

**Stir** and return it to the fire, grinding it, until it becomes prepared. It is "mortified" <term>mortificatio|the alchemical process of 'killing' a metal, or changing its chemical state so it loses its original properties, such as making mercury solid</term> by the wind <note>likely referring to the bellows or air flow</note> in a vessel, well-heated and slowly for four days in the furnace. This is the way of renewing the whiteness <note>original: "albītud̄"</note>, and then you will see it take on a redness.

**Because** of its humidity which can be distilled from it, you can lift it [from the heat] until it returns to a burnt red color <note>original: "rubīadustūm"</note>. Before this is done, the [substance] is heated and then placed upon a marble stone <note>used for cooling and grinding</note>. Through distillation it is finished and purified. This work is a long labor, and it is through this mortification that the substance is made ready to be coagulated.

# The Practice of Alchemy Begins, by Master Albertus Magnus

<margin>On salt</margin>
This work is here to teach the practice of alchemy. Concerning this, if you wish to know <margin>Alum</margin> <margin>more,</margin>
search the notes at the end of the following book for those things which are missing here and are found there. Regarding alum: take prepared alum, specifically 1 part saltpeter <term>salitre|saltpeter or potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in making corrosive acids</term> and [bitter] resin. Take 3 pounds and mix with cadmia <term>cadmie|zinc oxide or metallic soot collected from furnace walls</term>. Leave this for 3 hours, then place it in a glass vessel... over a fire... until it is turned into water. Remove it from the fire... [until it becomes] pale and clear. Fix it <term>fixation|the process of turning a volatile substance into a solid that can resist fire</term> with water... until it is clean. Distill it in a receiving vessel. This water is truly like the greenness of copper <note>original: "vrede aeris"; likely referring to verdigris or a similar copper-based solution</note>. Be careful when it has been distilled that it is coagulated <term>coagulation|thickening a liquid into a solid through cooling or evaporation</term> either by fire or by the sun. It will coagulate into the "noble salt" <note>original: "sal nobilis"</note> of this entire work. If at first it is not [pure], it should be dissolved again in a smaller quantity of water and distilled and coagulated again until it is good.
